title: Objects and Destructuring
summary: Object literals, property access, shorthand and destructuring.

steps.title: Object literals
body: In C# you declare a class before making an object. In JavaScript you write the object directly:
```ts
const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36, admin: false };
console.log(user.name);        // Ada
console.log(user["age"]);      // 36  (bracket access, key as a string)
user.age = 37;                 // const stops reassigning `user`, not changing it
TypeScript infers the shape `{ name: string; age: number; admin: boolean }`, and your editor then rejects `user.nmae` or `user.age = "old"`.
**Shorthand**: when a variable has the same name as the key, write it once:
```ts
const name = "Grace", age = 45;
const person = { name, age };   // { name: "Grace", age: 45 }
Reading a key that does not exist gives `undefined`, not an exception.

steps.explain: `const` does not freeze the object. A computed key reads `box.h`. A missing property is `undefined`. (TypeScript would underline `box.depth` in the editor, but Node only strips types, so it still runs.)

steps.title: Destructuring
body: Destructuring pulls properties out into variables, like C# deconstruction but by **name**:
```ts
const order = { id: 7, total: 1250, note: undefined };
const { id, total } = order;                 // id = 7, total = 1250
const { total: cents } = order;              // rename: cents = 1250
const { note = "none" } = order;             // default when undefined
Arrays destructure by **position**:
```ts
const [first, second] = ["gold", "silver", "bronze"];
let a = 1, b = 2;
[a, b] = [b, a];                             // swap
It works in parameters too, which is how React components read their props:
```ts
function label({ name, qty = 1 }: { name: string; qty?: number }) {
return `${qty} x ${name}`;

code: const { x, y: up, z = 0 } = point;
steps.explain: `y: up` renames, `z = 0` supplies a default, and an empty slot in `[p, , r]` skips an element.
